utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Kyle Wood, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson on behalf of General Rasim Delic. Our case manager is Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Just to remind you that you made a declaration at the beginning of your testimony last week to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the Defence and everyone else. Of course, I remember that. I abide by that sworn statement that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. So just to remind you that you are still bound by that declaration. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadziselimovic.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Just before we took the weekend recess, you had mentioned, at page 86, starting at line 19: "I think that there was a decision by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina where it was stated that all the Geneva Conventions were to be applied." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could have document P04050 displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you see that document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber what this is?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, this is a decree of the BH Presidency relating to the implementation of the International Laws of War within the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is this the law you were speaking of on Friday before the recess?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we looked at this decree on Friday. We spoke about the decision of the Presidency to apply the Geneva Conventions and about the criminal laws that were applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. This is a special decree in relation to the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers this into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our apologies. First of all, this document was tendered when Witness Delic testified and admitted. I think it might be a good idea to check, because we are duplicating a lot of our documents. I remember this document clearly. Secondly, we have a monitor problem here, Your Honours. We don't have the transcript. This should be 427, Exhibit 427, if the OTP could please check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say you don't have a transcript on your screen, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's right, Your Honours. We have a technical glitch over here, it seems, but the court deputy seems to be suffering from that same problem too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber's been advised that 427 is a signed version in a slightly different format and with a little more text on top. I'm not quite sure whether it's exactly identical to this. No text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 427. Let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's identical, but the document that the OTP are now tendering is a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, there's 427 on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our case manager has also checked into this. It does appear to be slightly different copies. The Prosecution is persuaded that the text is the same. It would be easier, I think, in this regard -- they have different ERN numbers as well. But if 427 could be shown to the witness, that would make things much easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 427 is on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I'll put that question to the witness now, then, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you withdraw P04050 now?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadziselimovic, does this appear to be the same as what you previously looked at, the document that was just on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We can move on then. This document can be put away, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document may be put away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadziselimovic, I want to take you into more specifics about the military -- District Military Prosecutor's Office. Can you tell me, sir, about how many cases did you handle during the war as a deputy District Military Court prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout my time with the Prosecution, once a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question again, sir. If you could remember, you told us you were a military prosecutor from 1993 to 1996. During that time, if you could tell the Court generally as a rough estimate, how many cases you handled, how many criminal cases you handled.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to say exactly what the figure was, but between 1.000 and 1.500 cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if you can tell the Trial Chamber generally, what was the majority of these cases about?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were cases where crimes against the armed forces were handled. That was in Articles 201 through 239 of the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Those were adopted, and that accounted for 60 per cent of the cases that we dealt with. The remaining cases had to do with what we termed "general crime," covering all the other crimes defined under the criminal law of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What were the most common criminal offences that you prosecuted during the war?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most common criminal offences had to do with crimes against property. That's what the chapter was called in the Criminal Code. Also, there was unauthorised departure from the armed forces or desertion, failure to obey orders, that sort of thing. It's difficult to remember now all of the crimes that were handled, but for the most part it was this type of crime that we dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Criminal reports that you received, did they come from -- only from military police or did they also come from civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible for both the military police and the civilian police to file criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, if a case was sent to the District Military Prosecutor's Office involving a person over which the district military prosecutor did not have jurisdiction, what would the Military Prosecutor's Office have done with that criminal case?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this was something that the district military prosecutor did not have jurisdiction over but, rather, a civilian prosecutor, for example, we would forward any such case to the appropriate prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If the police, when they went to the scene of a crime, after a preliminary investigation decided that the district military prosecutor did not have jurisdiction over the case, what would the police be obligated to do in that situation?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean civilian or military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. I mean the military police.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their responsibility was to file a criminal report. However, in practice, what I think was most often the case was that civilian police was contacted as soon as possible, especially if the investigation had been a joint one. So if at one moment it was decided that this was something for the civilian police, they would take over straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: When you say, sir, that their responsibility was to file a criminal report, what do you mean by that? Is that a legal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The law dictates that authorised officials had the responsibility of filing a criminal report whenever they came across evidence of a crime that was committed. It was the responsibility of each and every citizen, after all, to file a criminal report if there was anything to suggest that a crime was committed. This was a responsibility enshrined in the country's laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If document P02943 could be put on the screen, please. I see that document is coming up. Before we get to this, I do have one further question about the District Military Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You said in your testimony that you worked in that office until 1996. What happened in 1996 to the District Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there was a decision to abolish the military courts and military prosecutors. The same decision said that deputy military prosecutors and military prosecutor would be absorbed by the Higher Public Prosecutor Offices, and that's what happened to me. I was absorbed by the higher public prosecutor in Zenica, soon after which I was appointed deputy municipal public prosecutor in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What happened to all the archives and records of the District Military Prosecutor's Office when -- after 1996?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The district military prosecutor -- I'm speaking about Zenica now. That applied to all district military prosecutors throughout the country. I'm sorry. So in the decision abolishing military prosecutors, it was clearly envisaged what would happen to the files or, rather, to the cases being processed by district military prosecutors. The decision was made that the archives should be handed over to the appropriate public prosecutors throughout the country, meaning some of the cases might have been taken up by the higher public prosecutor in Zenica. Some of the cases might have been taken up by the municipal public prosecutors from throughout the country. As far as I remember, some of the cases were taken up by the Sarajevo higher public prosecutor. We were to hand over cases according to both real and territorial -- subject matter and territorial jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What happened specifically to the archives and records of the Zenica District Military Prosecutor's Office after 1996?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the archives was taken over by the civil prosecutor and the municipal prosecutor in Zenica, amounting to about between 60 and 70 per cent of the case-load.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what office has jurisdiction or has supervisory authority or custodian possession of those archives from the Zenica District Military Prosecutor's Office right now?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cantonal prosecutor of the Zenica-Doboj Canton, and I happened to be head of that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could turn to the document now. Do you recognise this document, Mr. Hadziselimovic?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We can see on the bottom of the version in Bosnian that there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel, can somebody scroll down, please, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And only to advance this second page to see the signature line, if that's what you have in mind, Mr. President. We can see, on the bottom of the Bosnian page and in the bottom of page 2 in the English version, there's a name, "Muris Hadziselimovic," and there's a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is that your signature, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, how did you go about producing this letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Hague Prosecutor requested that we hand over this information. If you look at the introduction from 1 to 2, Arabic 1 through 3, you will see that this was in fact the case. It was about the period between 1993 and 1996. I, as the chief prosecutor, ordered our archives to verify this information. A check was carried out, and based on that, this document was eventually produced. I endorsed this document with my signature. I confirm this document's authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, you say in your answer: "A check was carried out and our archives -- and based on that, this document was eventually produced." What archives or what records were checked in order for you to produce this letter?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about our archives, which comprised the archives of the former district military prosecutor in Zenica and the former higher public prosecutor in Zenica, as well as 10 municipal public prosecutors covered by this particular canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: You say "archives." What role did the registers that we talked about on Friday have in your search?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what we mean by "archives" is, above all, registers. All of those were inspected. Whenever we found a case, we would formally inspect it, so this included registers, logbooks, as well as individual case files, the check that I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And why would it be important to look at the registers when determining whether a particular criminal case had been received by the District Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're talking about the registers, this is something that's really important, because as I said on Friday, each case was registered in this kind of book. So, first of all, we would go through the registers. Whenever we found a case that was registered, it would always prove easy to track down. It never happened that we had a case that was not registered. That is why how the search took place is very important. First you look at the register and then you look at the logbook and then you look at individual case files.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could turn to the number 1 on that document, which is on page 1 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Under number 1, Mr. Hadziselimovic, we see that there are certain articles listed. Those are 36, 37, 38, 42, 52, 172 and 177 of the Criminal Code of BiH, as well as 142 to 146 of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia. Can you tell the Trial Chamber generally what Article 36 would have covered?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 36 was murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if you recall -- we can bring up these pages of the Code as well to assist if you don't recall, but if you recall generally, what did Article 37 cover?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 37 covered manslaughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If you could just take the Trial Chamber through the rest of those, 38, 42, 52 and the others. What did those articles cover, Mr. Hadziselimovic?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, 38, reckless endangerment. 42 was grievous bodily harm. 52 was unlawful detention. 172 was causing public danger, and 177 covered serious cases of causing public danger. I forget the name because there were three later amendments to these laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In any event, though, the document that we saw on Friday does explain what these laws are? That was the law that was in effect at the time; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but 140 through 146 covered war crimes. This is something that was adopted from the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. All these applied from 1993 to 1996, as the document reflects. 142 to 146.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, there are more pages of this, as we MIF'd it. There's a table, specifically. I see there at the top of the Bosnian version, it says "1 of 1". I don't know if there's any further pages beyond that. There are. If we could go to page 2 of the Bosnian version and just the final page. That would be, I'm sorry, page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you see that in front of you now, Mr. Hadziselimovic?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, is this an accurate reflection of a portion of the registers that you kept during the war?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire table reflects our records. I believe that each page has my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could just go through one particular entry just to get an idea of how things were recorded. Let's stick with the first one, for example, which appears to be under the first column. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, first of all, what "KT" means?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is simply the name of a register. This is where we kept cases with identified adult perpetrators of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In the first column there, there's a number. It says "33596". What is that number, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which number are you talking about, Mr. Wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Immediately beneath where it says "KP Vojno." I see that it's been highlighted now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Interpreter. Yeah, okay, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So specifically, Mr. Hadziselimovic, what does this "/96" indicate about this particular criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Registers were kept for each year individually. We would start with a new register with a new number at the beginning of the year, and we would conclude the register with the end of the year. Therefore -- excuse me. There should be "KT" just in front of the number and then "335/96". That would mean that within the KT register, this case was registered as case 335 in that year, that is, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And is that the same -- the same practice followed throughout the war and is it still followed today in your own registers, that a case would have a slash and then the year in which it was filed after it?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Moving to the second column immediately to the right, we see that it says: "CSB Zenica." Can you tell the Trial Chamber, what is CSB Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Centre of Security Services, Zenica, one of the organisational units of the civilian police. This should mean that they were the ones submitting the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And the third column labelled "Suspects," I believe that speaks for itself. If you look to the fourth column, there's a "36/2". Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that means?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that the crime in question is murder, Article 36(2) of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The column immediately after that, we have a translation here. It says "The injured party" or "victim." I want to draw your attention to the next column over. The heading in B/C/S, I believe it says "Ishod." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that is?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that 150890 -- well, it seems the case was transferred to the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Zenica perhaps in 1996. I cannot see it clearly. Yes, I can see it better. The 15th of August, 1996, the case was turned over to the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So in that entry, we see a "VJT." Immediately below that, we see "OJT." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what those initials stand for?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It stands for -- well, "VJT" is Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Zenica. "OJT" means Municipal Public Prosecutor's Office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And the next -- if we -- the next table down, if we could stay where we were, we see that there's an entry -- if we count six down, it says "KTM 1993". Can you tell the Trial Chamber what "KTM" stands for?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "KTM" is the register for criminal offences committed by minors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could go to the next page in B/C/S, and I will explain, Mr. President, that each individual entry has not been translated in this, but the headings have, so this amounts to the final page or one of the last final pages in the English. But I will take him through some of the entries in B/C/S at this point. And I apologise. If we could actually go to the next page in the B/C/S version. Now, we see -- if we could scroll up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: That entry at the top, that says "BVP Zenica." Can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, what does "BVP Zenica" stand for?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is another acronym for the Battalion of the Military Police, Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know, let me just interject here, Mr. Wood. I notice that these things that you are asking the witness to go through have not been translated on the English side. What are you expecting is going to happen at the time judgement is written? We're going to have to look at the B/C/S document to try and figure out what we have been told by the witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm told, Mr. President, that is the practice with respect to tables. One thing that can be done, I see that it wasn't with this document, but I know it has in others, and in particular the document that I'll be showing next, it does have a list of abbreviations that explains what those things stand for. We can have that produced for this one. I believe Mr. President is right, that it would be certainly helpful to have that done with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear you say this is the practice that is done. You know, if the practice doesn't answer to the problems -- address the problems, then maybe it's about time the practice was revisited. What's the point of giving us a translation if the translation is not identical to what is being translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I take your point, Your Honour, and we can have these particular acronyms translated. I believe you're right, that would be helpful. As I said, the next document that I show him, the witness will have those -- a list of acronyms and what they mean, the abbreviations and their translations. We can have that done with this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So are you saying we've got to refer to the list of acronyms and come back to the table when we arrive at judgement, or are you saying that the translations are going to be in the table?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What's been done, as you'll see in the next document, is that there's a list of acronyms at the back of the English translation of a cover letter that are the acronyms that are referred to throughout the table. This is typically how we get them back. They wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, your answer is the former of my two questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just say so, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. We will request a full translation of this document, Your Honour, that includes the tables and all the abbreviations and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wood. Finally, where are we going with this examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is to show the Trial Chamber a little bit of exactly how the records were kept, what records were indicated, and ultimately as we get to number 1 and then ultimately to number 2, this is to show exactly what criminal reports were filed with regard to the particular crimes at issue here. I'm taking the witness through this portion to explain the table to Mr. President and Your Honours and so that the Trial Chamber can get an idea of exactly what sort of search was done and can feel confident that the search was proper and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What sort of search was done or what kind of archiving was done?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Both, Your Honour, the records that were kept and how those records were searched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And in the fourth row, Mr. Hadziselimovic, we see that there's a "KTN." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what "KTN" stands for?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the name of the register with criminal offences committed by unknown or unidentified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All those abbreviations, the witness explained last week, KT, KTM, KTN. You're taking him through the same things again, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm taking him through these again so that Your Honours have an indication of how it looks and to remind Your Honours what these abbreviations stand for as they see them in the tables. I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could look at page 1 of the Bosnian version. And I believe we'll probably be looking at page 2 of the English version. This is at Roman numeral II. Yes, that's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziselimovic, you indicate in your letter here that there are no charges that were filed with regard to the following events. When you signed this letter, were you confident that this is an accurate reflection of what appeared in your archives?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. My clerks ran detailed checks, and since I trust them fully, I signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what criteria did you use in searching your archives to determine whether any crimes with regards to Arabic 1, 2 and 3 were referred to your office?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we were given a list of names of those killed. According to their names, we ran those checks in the appropriate registers. We didn't find a single case that was opened against known or unidentified perpetrators with any of the names from the list appearing in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 881.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could have document P06211. If we could advance to the page that's marked ERN 0613-2621. I believe it's a couple more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this document dated at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's dated 22 August 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What you see before you now, Your Honours, is the request from the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. I just want to see the date of the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could advance to the next page. The way this document was submitted, it's the -- first is the request from the prosecutor, and following that is the response from Mr. Hadziselimovic's office. It's the response that I'm most interested in. I believe that is page 3 of the Bosnian. It's beyond that even further. Perhaps page 4. Again, what we're seeing here is the --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Page 6, thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please zoom out? Can I see the following page, please? Yes, I recognise it now. This document was a reply to the prosecutor's request. It was signed by my deputy, since I was on annual leave at the time, and I authorised him to sign the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And these letters are similar, this letter and the last letter we saw. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what is the primary difference between them? That is to say, what is the different search of the archives you did to produce this letter than the search you did to produce the letter we saw just before?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period is important. The first document referred to 1993 to 1996, whereas this one pertains to the entire period up until end 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And did you use the same search criteria, Mr. Hadziselimovic, in both searches of the archives?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was the instruction I gave to my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: One notice -- one thing I noticed that's different, Mr. Hadziselimovic, that I wonder if you might be able to comment on. If we could go back to page 1 on the B/C/S again, and if we could stick with that page in the English, actually, the page we were on before it disappeared just then. And if we could scroll down in the Bosnian, I want to draw your attention, in particular, to the second bullet point that reads: "The killing and cruel treatment of three RS prisoners of war [Realtime transcript read in error "62 prisoners of war"] in the village of Livade [Realtime transcript read in error "Kesten"] or Kamenica camp, in the period 21 to 23 July 1993." [Realtime transcript read in error "11 to 19 September 1995"]. I believe if we looked at the request of the prosecutor, that date was actually 21 to 23 [Realtime transcript read in error "23 to 21"] July 1995, and I believe if we looked at the other letter, the search criteria was again 21 to 23 July 1995. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, what period was searched for this particular letter to be produced?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We ran our searches pertaining to the period between 1993 and 2000, including this period, as per request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could go back to the prosecutor's request. That would be the first page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, can I just intervene here? At page 20, line 21, you said, Mr. Prosecutor -- actually, 21 to 23 "July 1995". It's printed here "23 to 21". Just make sure that is corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. And, Mr. Wood, while you said "1995", I see the document there says "21 to 23 July 1993", so I'm not quite sure whether you're talking about 1995 or 1993. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll clarify this. If we could go to the first page of this document in both versions. And if we could actually go to the second page. The part of the request that's important is on the second page of both documents. And I want to draw your attention particularly to number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziselimovic, did you carry out the search as requested by the Prosecutor in this case?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We can see that the Prosecutor requested, under number two: "Murder and cruel treatment of three war prisoners, members of the Army of Republika Srpska in the village of Livade or on the Camp Kamenica in the territory of Zavidovici Municipality in the period from 21 to 23 July 1995 ..."?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we now explain why the other one says "1993"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber, sir, why the response from the prosecutor's office, from your office, indicates "21 to 23 July 1993", whereas the request from the Prosecutor from the OTP was from 21 to 23 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain that with any degree of certainty, but what I can tell you is that the entire period between 1993 and 2000 was checked. I suppose that this was merely a typographical error. It reads "1993" by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 882.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziselimovic, during your time as a deputy District Military Court prosecutor, do you remember there being any criminal reports or prosecutions involving any crimes coming out of the Kamenica Camp, what is called "the Kamenica Camp"?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you with certainty that I did not handle such cases. As you said, yourself, I was deputy district military prosecutor. The district prosecutor -- district military prosecutor would know for sure whether there were any such cases, if he were here. I cannot tell you anything as to whether there was such a case received by the District Military Prosecutor's Office at the time, since I was not the head of the office at the time. If we go back to the document we've just seen, I can tell you that we did not receive any such cases, that is, it wasn't received by our military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, there's something that I don't understand from the answer that comes. I thought, when you took us through the exercise of your registers here, you were trying to show to us that you searched, using your registers during that time, the time covered by the time when you were a deputy prosecutor, military prosecutor, and that therefore, according to the records of that office, you give an answer. Now, when you say you were merely a deputy, "the prosecutor, if he were here, could answer better," I got a bit lost. I thought you've told us what the prosecutor would have told us. Did I miss something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As deputy district military prosecutor, I was not responsible for the registers and what was being entered. That is why, personally, I cannot tell you whether anything was entered or not. But from the point of view of the chief prosecutor of the cantonal office in Zenica, where I was also responsible for the archives of the former District Military Prosecutor's Office, I can tell you that what we were asked to carry out searches on was not found. However, I cannot tell you the same thing pertaining to Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could ask a follow-up question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, the question I asked you was about whether you personally remembered. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, are you confident, sir, that if a case had been filed with -- under the criteria that are listed in your responses to the requests of the prosecutor, would it appear in the registers?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had a criminal report been submitted, it would have been entered into the register, and as such, there would be a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The other question I have is: On page 24, line 4, you say: "However, I cannot tell you the same thing pertaining to Zavidovici." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What District Military Prosecutor's Office had territorial jurisdiction over Zavidovici Municipality in 1993 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The District Military Prosecutor's Office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So it follows, then, if a criminal report had been filed for an event occurring in Zavidovici Municipality involving military personnel, it would have been filed into the Zenica District Military Prosecutor's Office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And it follows from that, then, that if such a report had been filed, it would appear in the registers and in the archives that your staff had searched when you produced these letters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The Prosecution has no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Madam Vidovic, but I thought that we should conclude the Prosecution's examination-in-chief by asking the witness about the possible reasons why no official record was ever made of the incidents that are mentioned in the Prosecution's letter. I realise one option is that the witness never heard of these incidents before they were introduced to him in the Prosecution's letters, and another option would be that these incidents never took place. So my question to the witness is if you ever heard of these incidents while you were serving as a prosecutor in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning the murders referred to here, I had never heard of them before I was contacted by the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I guess that settles my questions. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadziselimovic. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and I will cross-examine you today on behalf of General Rasim Delic. I would kindly ask you that you pause before answering, and I will do the same with my questions, so that the transcript could accurately reflect our discussion. Most of my questions can be answered by saying "yes" or "no," and I'm sure you're familiar with the nature of cross-examination, for that matter. You gave us some information on your career. I will not go through those questions again, but I wanted to ask you this: It is correct, is it not, that you were a member of the War Presidency of the former municipality of Kotor Varos or, rather, the Municipality of Kotor Varos in exile, until March 1993?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. In March 1993, I was appointed a member of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, you were a member of the War Presidency, of this War Presidency in exile. The thrust of my question is this, actually: You know how war presidencies in exile functioned; don't you?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us you were deputy district military prosecutor in Zenica from the 1st of April, 1993, until July 1996, when District Military Courts ceased their work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was your boss, his first and last name? Who was the chief district military prosecutor at the time?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of 1992 until, I believe, 1995, the middle of that year, it was Kemal Mularifovic, succeeded by Sefedin Suljevic until District Military Prosecutor's Offices were abolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those two people are alive, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was a regulation in place by which the cases of the District Military Prosecutor's Office were taken over by the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, inter alia, or among others.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The same process was conducted when it came to the issue of District Military Courts, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about the status of cases of the District Military Prosecutor's Office and the Court in Travnik. When the District Military Court in Travnik was closed down, the cases of the District Military Prosecutor's Office and the Court were taken over by the Higher Court in Zenica, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, even today the Court in Travnik, as well as the prosecutor's office there, functioned as departments of the Cantonal Court in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In any case, these cases which existed during the war, including any potential criminal reports, investigations, indictments issued by the District Military Prosecutor's Office in Zenica were taken over by the Travnik institutions; isn't that so? I believe that is clear.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not completely. I need to explain, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is as follows: The District Military Prosecutor's Office in Zenica had territorial jurisdiction. The Municipalities of Travnik and the other ones I mentioned on Friday, that situation existed until the Military District Prosecutor's Office in Travnik was founded.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziselimovic, I would like to stop you here. Tell us when exactly the District Military Prosecutor's Office in Travnik was formed.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you what year exactly, unfortunately, as I said on Friday. I believe it was 1993, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will go back to the Travnik cases again, but I want to move on to something else right now. During the war, anyone could submit a criminal report, even an ordinary citizen. However, I'm interested in any potential activities of the relevant bodies in that regard. As you said, criminal reports could also be submitted by security organs, civilian and military ones; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian and military police, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That certainly included the Military Security Service, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I note the time. Perhaps this is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately we have to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis again because again Judge Harhoff has had to go to the Milosevic case. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution had concluded its questions. I believe Madam Vidovic had the floor when we took the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We talked about those filing criminal reports. After whoever is filing a criminal report has filed that criminal report, this person no longer wields any influence over the proceedings, do they?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So from that moment on, it's down to the appropriate prosecutor and court to see what measures need taking, in terms of prosecuting whoever is suspected of having committed a crime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but this was the responsibility of whoever the appropriate prosecutor happened to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You mean the chief prosecutor or -- I didn't quite get your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief prosecutor was responsible for prosecuting, yes. And needless to say, in certain trials he would have his own deputies who would press on with the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So a prosecutor could start proceedings having received a criminal complaint, but they could also throw out any criminal complaints that they received, or maybe there was an investigation, after which charges were dropped; those were possibilities, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was down to the prosecutor to legally define any possible crimes? Whoever filed the complaint did not have the authority to categorise or classify crimes into legal terms?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even just learning of a possible crime, without the criminal complaint being filed, meant that a prosecutor was responsible to take measures to see who the perpetrator might have been and what the crime might have been that was committed or possibly committed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is not entirely true.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please elaborate on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll do my best. The law contains, indeed, the provision that you allude to in your question. The prosecutor, however, did not technically have the authority to carry out an order or perhaps order an investigation to anyone, so that knowledge of a crime that was committed did not, in practical terms, allow for the possibility to immediately launch proceedings. Why? Because the basic jurisdiction of any prosecutor is to prosecute possible perpetrators, but it didn't have anything to do with discovering that a crime was committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right if I stated this: Only if any rumour reached the prosecutor that a crime had been committed would he have been under an obligation to order the appropriate authorities to start pre-trial proceedings; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not what was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe that was not the done thing in the Zenica area, but you will agree with me, surely, that this was a provision, a legal provision, and the provision itself is crystal clear about what it says; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't quite agree, because the provision, the way you interpret it, did not exist. It wasn't consistently phrased like that. There was a possibility that existed, but this was by no means a commitment or an obligation. It is said should any rumours reach the prosecutor, they may or may not choose to start proceedings. That, at least, is my recollection of the wording.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness please be shown D713. Your Honours, could we please look at page 4 of the document, the Bosnian. Page 3 in the English. Could we please focus on the right-hand page. That's right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at paragraph 2. You will agree that this is what it says: "If the public prosecutor is unable to determine on the face of a criminal report whether the allegations in the report are probable, or if the information in the report does not provide a sufficient basis needed to decide whether to request an investigation, or if --" And now this is the bit that is relevant for our purposes: " ... Or if the public prosecutor has only heard that a crime may have been committed, and particularly the perpetrator is unknown, the public prosecutor, the public prosecutor, if unable to do so himself or through other organs, shall request the internal affairs organs to gather the necessary information and take other measures toward uncovering the criminal act and the perpetrator." You will therefore agree that this is an obligation enshrined in the law on criminal prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree. It says "may," and that is a possibility or an option, but no obligation or commitment. When talking about the prosecutor, obviously the reference here is to the chief prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is not a dilemma for us. I'm talking about the chief prosecutor, but I don't see the word "may." It reads: "The prosecutor shall request ...," does it not?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the very last sentence: "The public prosecutor can or may always request the internal affairs to inform him ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To inform him of any measures taken. That's a different thing, but I'm talking about launching an investigation; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The matter at stake is really this: How does one prove that a prosecutor has heard rumours of a crime being committed? This always needs to be in writing, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much, Witness. Your Honours, can this document please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 883.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can put this document away for the time being. Thank you. I want the witness to look at Exhibit 882 now, please. It was shown to the witness today by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before we see that document, let me ask you a number of questions to do with the reports that you forwarded to the Prosecutor about crimes that you enumerated, 36, 37, 38, Article 42, 52, 172, 177, of the Criminal Law of Bosnia and Herzegovina, crimes, 142 through 146 of the Criminal Law of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was adopted. That relates to war crimes; right? You remember looking at this document today, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Go back to page 1, please, and then I'll be asking you to go to page 2. Your Honours, I wish to ask a number of questions about both of these documents, the documents used by the Prosecutor today, and at times this might require that the witness go through the documents. That's why we have hard copies available to the witness, whereas we ourselves can follow what is going on on our screens, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor specifically asked you, as he explained, to go through certain documents - registers, case files - in order to see whether any reports, investigations or indictments were received or were recorded that have to do with trials here before this Tribunal. On the 28th of October -- of August, you wrote a letter to the OTP about that. I want the witness to look at page 6 now of that letter in both the Bosnian and the English. The reference is page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was the letter on the 28th or on the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 22nd of August, Your Honour. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You explained that in your letter dated the 13th of October, 2006, you forwarded information about these crimes in the period between 1993 and 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Madam Vidovic. Now the transcript talks of 13th of October, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a different letter that I'm talking about dated the 13th of October, which I will be invoking later on. I'm just trying to create a link between these two documents. It's a shortcut that I'm taking, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you said "yes," did you not? All right, we'll get to that. You confirmed the authenticity of the information, for the most part, contained in both these documents that you were shown by the OTP today?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You explained that you forwarded to them a table or a chart about criminal complaints received between the 1st of January, 1996, and the 31st of December, 2000; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in the letter that is dated the 22nd of August, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I'm talking about. I'll be going back to that document, but right now we can leave this one aside. And I want the witness to look at Exhibit 881, please. So this is a letter, the letter that we talked about a while ago, the 24th of October, 2006. Please look at Roman II on the first page. You said that: "In the aforementioned archives there were no files or other documents which would indicate that the following was carried out: Submission of criminal reports, investigation of pressing of charges, related to the following events." And then there's a list. We see, back in 1993, something that occurred in Maline/Bikosi, the village of Maline/Bikosi the 8th of June, 1993. There is murder and mistreatment of POWs, members of the Army of Republika Srpska. So this is all in relation to 1995 under "2"; right? Can you please now go to page 2 of the Bosnian, and this is page 3 in the English. The Prosecutor showed you these tables or boxes. I won't be spending a lot of time with this, but what I'm putting to you is this: I've gone through this document, the document which you now have in front of you, so you can just leaf through it, for your benefit. There is some information there, and aside from some exceptions, this is information from the register, the register which lists known perpetrators of crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but there's also the KTN register and there's a special register for known crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please go to page 4 of the document in the Bosnian. The same in English. Page 3 in the English, as a matter of fact. It's the one with the boxes and columns. Can you please focus on "KTN Military," "KTN Military." You say that you went through this record; right? This relates to unknown perpetrators or unidentified perpetrators. If one goes through this report that you wrote, the inference one can draw is as follows: Between the 8th of June, 1992, and the 1st of January, 1996, according to this information, at least, a mere 12 criminal reports were received against unidentified perpetrators in relation to these crimes, all forms of murder, endangering another person's safety, unlawful detention, that sort of thing. Is it your evidence that you went through the KTN registers relating to unknown perpetrators for this period of time and this is all you found? You found no other criminal reports in relation to unknown perpetrators, other than these listed here? That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The table states "KTN Military." The cases that were recorded in the KTN register of the district military prosecutor. "Unknown perpetrators," that is stated in each of the boxes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear you and the witness talk of "KTN Military," and I do see on the B/C/S "KTN Vojno" or something like that. But on the English, we see "KT," "KTN" and "KT", so it doesn't look like we're on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please look at the first box? It says "KTN" -- or the first column on the left, "KTN, Unknown Military." Did you see that? The first column, the first table, and it reads "KT" -- yes, Your Honour, you're quite right. There's an error in the English. You're right, and thank you for that. It should read "KTN." There's an "N" missing there. That's what I have been discussing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's my problem, because I don't have the "N" on the English. That's why I couldn't follow you. Okay. Anyway, now this is "KT" on the first box on top is supposed to be "KTN Military," "Unknown perpetrators in the military"?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I'm with you. Do you know that, Mr. Wood? Mr. Wood? Mr. Wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. This document, the English translation will be revised, and we'll produce a final version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's do that. Thank you very much. You may proceed. I'm sorry, Madam Vidovic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it is your evidence that in those registers, between the 8th of June, 1993, and the 1st of January, 1996, there were a mere 12 criminal complaints relating to unknown perpetrators for these crimes; is my understanding correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain, please?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are KTN cases that were recorded in the KTN register. Therefore, perpetrators of these crimes remain unidentified. Every time a perpetrator was identified, the case would be transferred to the KT register, the register for known perpetrators. What this means is that these particular perpetrators remained unidentified. That's all it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that particular clarification. Let's assume this: I go to the Zenica archive and I find a case file from 1993 which is recorded as "Unknown perpetrator, KTN," I'll always be able to find it there, right, regardless of whether it's still on the unknown list, unidentified, or whether a name has been assigned to it because a perpetrator has been found; is that what you're saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that over this two-and-a-half-year period, you did not receive a single criminal report against any unknown or unidentified perpetrator for a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Known or unknown?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Unknown.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that it's not stated on this list. What this means is that perhaps there was something like that, but then it became KT over time, which means that the perpetrator was found. Unknown perpetrator for a war crime, yes, that would have been on a list like this, so it is likely that a criminal report was filed, but then the perpetrator was found, and in the meantime the case file became KT, known perpetrator. That's the only possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In which case we would be able to find it on one of your lists?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, marked as "KT, known perpetrator."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay, talking about war crimes, there's one thing I want you to clarify, your letter of the 24th of October, 2006. You write in your reply to the OTP there are no case files or other documents that would indicate that criminal reports were received or any requests for investigation or any charges brought for the killings at Maline. You were quite clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please go to page 3 of this document, the Bosnian version of this document. Your Honour, it seems that this page was not translated at all. It seems that this document had only two pages translated. I apologise. It wasn't what I would expect to find. It was not a large document, and I thought the whole of it would be translated. However, I will ask the witness to clarify, as I believe it needs some clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On page 3, the seventh row from below, we can see that there was an investigation, the number of which was K33/01 or 014/2000, against Besim Spahic concerning the events in the villages of Maline and Bikosi. Do you see that? At this moment, it is the third line from the bottom on the screen. Your Honours I will read out so that you can follow, or perhaps the witness can do that. Can you see that? The third column, Besim Spahic, Articles 141 and 142, that is war crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you read what follows, "Zenica Municipality" and then the rest?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Zenica Municipality, the 26th of January to the 31st of December, 1993." I believe it says "Dusina, Miletici, Susanj, Ovnak, Maline and Bikosi."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please read out the next column.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next one?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now you can see it better. It's towards the middle of the screen. It says "Return from The Hague ..."?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "Return from The Hague, forwarded to" --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "BH"?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 5th of January 2006." It should actually read: "Forwarded to the prosecutor's office in B and H," I believe, since the date is the 5th of January, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you have this piece of information in mind when answering the Prosecutor's questions yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't recall the whole table, but I believe I had that piece of information in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under that, we have "Ki 37/01, Enver Hadzihasanovic, Article 141", and then it reads: "Returned from The Hague."

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Roman rules of the road, that case was forwarded to The Hague and then returned. I believe it was forwarded to the Prosecutor's Office of B and H, since they handle all communication between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Hague Tribunal, and it could be the case was transferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just so that everyone would understand, when it says "according to the rules of the road according to the Treaty of Rome," it means that the organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina forwarded certain case files to The Hague Prosecutor so that it would be assessed there in keeping with the agreement, that is, to see whether certain people could be processed according to international standards; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to page 4 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the bottom part of the table. That's the right one. Four cases are mentioned of war crimes. That was the separate register you had for war crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a separate register with the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have four case files concerning war crimes, and I will ask you some questions about it somewhat later, but let us please move on to the next page now, or perhaps Their Honours can leaf through it, through their hard copy. Witness, would you agree with me that there are no war crimes case files on the next page?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is Article 142, for Their Honours. Could we please go to the next page. And then page 9. On this page, look at -- well, look at the first name, "Vinko Vidovic," a person suspected of having committed a war crime, and you would agree with me he is not a Bosniak, judging by his first and last name?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, he is Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We can see that the MP Battalion submitted a criminal report against that person, and now let us go down towards the middle of the page, "383/93". We can also see that there is mention of the MP Battalion. They submitted a criminal report against Mirko Vlajic for a war crime. That person is not a Bosniak, either, would you agree, since his first and last name are not Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There are two names that follow pertaining to war crimes from the Higher Court in Zenica. We have Dzemal Zahirovic, Article 142. This person is a Bosniak, is he not? And please remember this name.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he is a Bosniak, judging by the first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The things we've been through so far, according to the report, one would say that the District Prosecutor's Office, for the relevant period specified in the letter, received six reports on war crimes committed, with the exception of those mentioned on page 1. That is what one would conclude, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely whether this is actually the district public prosecutors or the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office, since it is the same archives. These two prosecutor's offices were the only ones competent to process war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Meaning both prosecutors' offices in total received six cases, this is the way we should read it, they received six criminal reports in both offices?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is so, pertaining to this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to page 6, please. There is an Arabic name. I believe it will be easy for you to spot it. Please go down. It's 236/95. There is Rasid Alsudarji, Sead Alubeidi, Article 50, that is kidnapping. Do you know what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In relation to the whole of the report, I wanted to ask you this: Again, did you go through all of the registers concerning unknown perpetrators of crimes in 1993, 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, my service did that on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your service go through the KTA registers concerning specific events during those years which, for example, could contain Maline and Bikosi?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can put this document away, and I'd like to show PT2962 to the witness. This is correspondence between The Hague Prosecutor's Office and -- let us go to page 3, please, and it will be clear. The Hague Prosecutor requested certain information. Your Honours, there is another problem here, because the translation is not organised in the right way, and it is difficult to follow it. However, I'm interested in one detail only.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a letter of the Travnik Prosecutor's Office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Madam Vidovic, the documents on the screen don't look alike. I'm not quite sure -- the one side is a letter. The other side is a table.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Thank you for your effort. I'm interested in this page only.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we can see here that the Cantonal Office, Prosecutor's Office in Travnik, is informing the prosecutor that -- you can see it under Roman numeral II, that they do have a case file for Enver Hadzihasanovic and 32 other persons. The number is KT 56/99, war crimes. It has to do with people killed in the villages of Maline and Bikosi. I wanted to ask you this: We saw that on your list, there was also a case against -- a case file for Enver Hadzihasanovic. However, we see here that reference is made of the Cantonal Travnik Prosecutor's Office. We can see that there -- there was a mention of the same case on two occasions, but however, one cannot have two different proceedings in the same case; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, is this the same case or did the Travnik Prosecutor's Office have an investigation of their own and you had one on your part pertaining to these events, another case file, another case? Perhaps you can explain.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything for certain. At the time, and this is 1999 or perhaps 1998, I was not with the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Zenica, and they had jurisdiction over cases such as this. Therefore, without reviewing the case file, I cannot tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that you did not study this case file or the other two case files you saw on the list for Enver Hadzihasanovic or for Besim Spahic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This case file from the Travnik Cantonal Office, well, I couldn't have any insight into that, and I couldn't study the material pertaining to the other Prosecutor's Office. In the other case, before the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Zenica, I also had no insight into that, since we did not have that case file. It was with The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But the BH organs forwarded it to The Hague Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. At that time, I didn't occupy that position. However, I presumed that it was so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we assign an exhibit number to this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is given an exhibit number -- I beg your pardon, is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 884.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can put the document away. I'd like to show 2919 to the witness, P2919. This is correspondence between the federal Minister of Justice of the Federation of B and H and the Cantonal Court in Zenica. I just wanted you to see that. Please go to page 4 of the document in the Bosnian. I believe we'll have the same problem as before again. This page has not been translated, but what I am interested in has, and it is also on page 4 in the English. No, sorry, on the first page of the English. This is fine. The English is fine.
