Please let us go to page 4 in the Bosnian. Actually, the fifth page in the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziselimovic, we can see here that the president of the Cantonal Court in Zenica, on the 10th of May, 2002, is forwarding information pursuant to the request of the 28th of March, 2002. The president enumerates the judges that worked during that period. I believe you're familiar with the names. Do you know that these judges indeed worked at that time?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. She's also mentioning data on any proceedings for war crimes. Look at the last two paragraphs. The last paragraph in English, Your Honours. You can see the names we just saw in your report, Mirko Vlajic, we saw that one, member of the HVO. Then -- is that so?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the next page, please, in the English. And in Bosnian, Witness, you can see that there's also Dzemal Zahirovic mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These two case files are mentioned. We've seen these two names in your report. You see here "Dzemal Zahirovic." He's a Bosniak, you said, isn't that so, and he was accused of having committed war crimes in the Batkovic camp. When it comes to war crimes, so as to have no misunderstanding, when answering the Prosecutor's questions concerning Article 142, which has to do with war crimes against civilians, you've explained that there was also an offence called a war crime committed against prisoners. Is it true that such crimes have their bases in the violations of the International Humanitarian Law; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was specific and particular concerning the Criminal Code of the SFRY when these offences are concerned, anyone could be held responsible for having committed a war crime, provided that person either ordered or perpetrated, committed a violation of the International Humanitarian Law and the people who are protected by such legislation?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I said on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the Criminal Code of the SFRY did not foresee any responsibility on the part of the commander in order to prevent and punish the perpetrators of such crimes?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Criminal Code of the SFRY that was taken over by Bosnia-Herzegovina did not mention the issue of command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as applied in the war, had no mention of superior command responsibility in failing to act following certain crimes committed by their subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Command responsibility, as is understood and treated by The Hague Tribunal, well, no, the Code did not contain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That type of responsibility was put into the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina only after the war, when the State Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, since that law is only applied by the Prosecutor's Office and the State Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I wanted to ask you this: Commanders responsibility, in terms of failing to act, it was made part of the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina only after the war? That is what I was asking you.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat my answer. I don't know. I am not the one who applies that law in practice. That law from 2003 is only applied by the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't have to be familiar with that law.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in that -- or, rather, in the year of 2006, your Prosecutor's Office submitted a criminal report against Sabahudin Opert, et al based on that particular provision, based on the issue of command responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't quite agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Partially, you would, I presume. What is it that you wouldn't agree with?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The institution of command responsibility, as such, is only applied by The Hague Tribunal. Therefore, we used only that part of the article in which there is mention of someone ordering that things be carried out. Therefore, a superior can order something and then be held responsible. He -- also, the perpetrator is responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if you receive a case file, if a report was filed to you for a war crime in terms of command responsibility, how would you determine whether your office is competent or not if you are not familiar with the law? That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that it was actually not being familiar with the organisation of the judiciary in Bosnia-Herzegovina made you ask me such a question. The exclusive competence to institute proceedings for war crimes lies with the Prosecutor's Office of B and H.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will tell you that at the level of Cantonal Prosecutor's Offices there are countless investigations into such crimes. However, I don't want to dwell on this issue any further. I wanted to ask you something about your testimony today. However, I am telling you that it is precisely at this moment there are criminal reports about such crimes with all Cantonal Prosecutor's Offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I don't see a question here. What I see is, "I want to tell you something." This sounds as if -- I object to the form of the question, Your Honour. It sounds as if Madam Vidovic is actually testifying here and badgering the witness, and on these grounds I would object to this question being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to suggest to the witness that at this moment there are numerous investigations into such crimes. However, I don't want to dwell on this anymore. I believe I would lose much time. I want to go back to this document, and of course I withdraw my question so as not to waste any additional time. Could we please turn the next page of the document in the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In case we turn the English page as well, can I just get confirmation, did I hear that Mr. Vinko Vidovic is not Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On this same page, please look at paragraph 3, from the bottom up. I quote -- it is the same paragraph in the English. It reads: "With regard to BH Army members, according to the records of this court, not a single case was tried in the period in question, nor during the court's existence." So, Witness, in other words, according to this report, for as long as the Zenica District Military Court existed, based on these reports by you and the president of that Court, it would seem that a single Bosniak was prosecuted, a Muslim, as we find stated there, and even that Bosniak was not even a member of the army. That's the conclusion that we might reach, having read your reports. Would you say that that's true?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My signature is there, which means I confirm that it is true. I assume it to be consistent with what the president of the Court stated as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that was Ms. Alihodzic, right, Zijada Alihodzic?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Can we please have a number for this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 885.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now, Your Honours, I want to show the witness D705.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a document produced by the district military prosecutor in Travnik. The date is the 29th of August, 1995. It was sent to the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It reads: "Military District Prosecutor Sead Zeric." Based on what you know, is this a person who late in 1995 worked as a military prosecutor in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, my understanding was the Zenica prosecutor took over the cases previously handled by the Travnik military prosecutor. Right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you asked me that before the break, I told you you weren't entirely right in that respect. The cases handled by the Travnik district military prosecutor were taken over by the cantonal prosecutor of the Central Bosnia Canton.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and what you're trying to say is these cases have nothing whatsoever to do with your Prosecutor's Office; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Be that as it may, is it your evidence that you don't know who the district military prosecutor in Travnik was in 1995? You probably worked together in one way or another, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Worked together, sure, but let me remind you that I was a deputy military prosecutor, and that being my role, I was not supposed to know who it was. And, indeed, at the time I did not know who the district military prosecutor was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this: It was quite usual for a prosecutor to inform the Ministry of Justice on certain issues; right? You accept that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Written reports or annual reports were normally submitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, either one of those; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So what's important here and the reason I'm showing you the report is this: If you can read it, you can see that the district military prosecutor in Travnik was requested to provide information on how many proceedings were underway against Muslims or Bosniaks for genocide or war crimes, and this district military prosecutor from Travnik replies: "Please note that in the preceding period, we received three criminal reports against such persons ..." Bosniaks and Muslims, that is what he means. " ... And these were referred to the Zenica Senior Prosecutor's Office as the court having subject-matter and territorial jurisdiction." Okay. Now, what I wish to ask you is this: This document obviously says that three criminal reports against Muslims or Bosniaks were forwarded to Zenica on the 29th of December, 1995. Did you bear in mind those three criminal reports against Muslims or Bosniaks when you put together that report, the report -- the two reports that you submitted to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to be able to answer accurately, I would have to explain a little about the situation concerning the hand-over of archives or case files. This is how it works: The military district prosecutor in Zenica and the military district -- district military prosecutor in Travnik were functioning for a while until they were abolished. They had territorial jurisdiction and subject-matter jurisdiction was the same exactly, but territorial depended on their territory. It roughly covers what today we know as cantons in B and H. At the same time, the authority of the civilian bodies, that is, the senior public prosecutor in this case, is to cover the entire territory covered by these two district prosecutors. In this situation, it is possible that the three criminal reports were submitted to the senior public prosecutor in Zenica, but it is far more likely or even certain that the three reports were, I assume, in relation to the territorial jurisdiction of the Travnik Canton. When the Cantonal Prosecutor's Office was first set up in Travnik, these cases, I assume, were submitted to that prosecutor, the civilian prosecutor. So the way this is organised, this is a bit complicated, but I assume that that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Be that as it may, be that as it may, Mr. Hadziselimovic, do you agree that these three criminal reports were not something that we saw in your chart, in your report? No way that report, the two documents that you were shown by the OTP today?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about. I don't know what criminal reports these are, specifically, but if it's confirmed in the report, in the letter, that these were submitted to the senior public prosecutor, well, then they might as well have been registered. If we came across such a case file in the archive of the senior public prosecutor, we would know. Now, how did this happen? If we had the names contained in these reports, we could check; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you agree that these are three Muslims, Bosniaks, and having gone through your report in its entirety, we tracked down no more than a single Muslim; right? So what I'm trying to say is that these three criminal reports were never submitted, although according to this document, they reached Zenica. Would you accept that? Would you accept at least the possibility that this happened, that they simply weren't registered, for God knows what reason?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I very much doubt that they were simply not registered. We looked at that table and we saw that there was the report against Besim Spahic, so that might have been one of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that precisely is what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't know. I don't have names, therefore --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter didn't hear the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Prosecutor, you do agree that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said this might have been the report against Besim Spahic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that what the witness said? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it may have been the report against Besim Spahic or against Enver Hadzihasanovic, because those were the two that we found in the report. However, I don't have the names and I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, could we please have a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 886.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, D610, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As we're waiting for this document, Besim Spahic was the head of the Zenica Municipality, the wartime head; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think so. It's not exactly what the position was called, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But it was someone from the civilian structures; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please look at this document, sir. This is a criminal report by the Security Services Centre in Zenica. This was submitted to the senior public prosecutor in Zenica on the 1st of February, 1994. You will agree, if you look at the names here, if you look at the information, you will see that these are three Arabs, based on the information contained in this criminal report. Two of them were actually members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. And the criminal report was submitted to the senior public prosecutor in Zenica. Can we just lower the document slightly so we can see the date, please. Right, thank you. It was submitted on the 31st of February, 1994 -- I'm sorry, the 1st of February, 1994. I'm sorry. These persons were suspected of having committed the crime of murder under Article 35 or, rather, 36, paragraph 2, of the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The number is not really all that legible, is it? So these are members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. You will agree that this criminal report was never submitted to the district military prosecutor, rather it was submitted to the senior prosecutor, right, civilian prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document shows.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I will provide a page reference, Your Honour. 6129 of the transcript, lines 20 through 25, and page 6130, lines 1 through 7. That's the reference in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said the military courts was responsible for prosecuting and trying members of the BH Army, unless there were civilian co-perpetrators who committed certain crimes with some of the soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. What we see stated here is two members of the El Mujahid Detachment and a third person who appears to be a civilian, an ethnic Arab. We see that the criminal report was submitted. If we could please lower the document so we can see the header. By the Security Services Centre. If we could please just lower slightly. All right. The Bosnian, too, yes please. Thank you. Okay, Security Services Centre submitted this report to a civilian prosecutor. I believe you know about this particular case, which is the murder of Paul Godal, a member of the ODA Humanitarian Organisation. You ever heard of anything like that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it does ring a bell, but I wasn't with the senior public prosecutor at the time. Therefore, I'm not familiar with the detail of this case. It does ring a bell, though. I did hear of it at the time, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So this was taken to the senior public prosecutor. You are aware of this, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd much sooner say that I heard about this somewhere off the record, but I didn't know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. There was a scandal that erupted over this case because these persons escaped at one stage during their trial; right? Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does ring a bell. I heard of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So what I think is relevant, in terms of your evidence, relevant for our purposes, is this: I looked carefully through your letters. You were asked about the crime of murder. You were asked to go through the registers of the senior prosecutor and the military prosecutor. Do you agree with me that this is not a report that you recorded, although it quite certainly was tried and you know it? It was tried, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't find these persons or this case in the table, then I didn't state that, did I? However, I do see this criminal report in front of me right now. It should have been recorded in the register of the senior public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we might want to have our break now, and I'll just ask the witness -- he has both these reports that the Prosecutor was showing him today. I'll ask him to go carefully, through the break, through both of these documents so we may be able to ascertain whether this report is in fact mentioned in any of his reports or not. Could we please have a number assigned to this document for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 887.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would that then be a convenient time, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break until half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We were talking about the criminal report against those three persons, Security Services Centre of Zenica, senior public prosecutor Abdullah Abtani [phoen] and others. We asked the witness to go through his own reports during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have you had a look at the two letters that we discussed, your reports to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I have, and I can explain as follows: I had two minutes to -- I had ten minutes to look at them, and I didn't find the names from that criminal report, as stated previously. I think the reason is as follows: As the Defence stated at the beginning of this cross, the OT -- the prosecutor was never bound by the legal qualification of a crime by the police. I think what happened in this particular case was this: The senior public prosecutor received this criminal report, and their legal view of the matter was probably different from that stated in the original criminal report. It may have been categorised as abduction under Article 50, the crime itself, but no requests were made to check anything in relation to that article, and that is why the names are missing from the table that was attached to the letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you just said, that's merely an assumption on your part, isn't it? You did not see the case file, did you?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We cannot avoid drawing the following inference, based on your response: If the body in charge of pre-trial -- in charge of an investigation, be it a military body or a civilian body, filed a certain criminal report containing the description of a crime, and the crime was described, and if found differently, and this is not something that the prosecutor originally had brought up, in such cases we would not find these cases listed on your list; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're right, because requests were raised in relation to specific crimes that were defined in a specific way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But would it not be true, in fact, if I suggested this: As soon as a criminal report reaches a prosecutor, it is entered into the register with all the original descriptions contained in the original report. For example, Security Services Centre reports Abdullah Abtani and others for the crime of murder, as soon as it is registered the prosecutor is still in no position to change the legal description and definition of a crime contained therein; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not entirely right, because the chief prosecutor marks whatever articles are to be entered or registered. At the top of that criminal report, he marks the article under which a certain criminal report is to be subsumed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right, I see. So somebody says "war crime," but they might as well end up writing just "murder"; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Defence is suggesting something that is not quite right; therefore I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you just said that he is the person in charge of actually amending something. This is a serious crime, the crime of murder being reported here, and according to what you are saying, it was later defined as abduction, which is a much less serious crime, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about any assessments that someone may have made back in 1994. All I'm trying to explain is how it could have happened that these persons were not listed on that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you how this really happened, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you a different question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do, can we just scroll up the English in the -- thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this, suppose a security organ, civilian police, let's assume that for the time being, believed that the perpetrator was a member of a paramilitary unit, a paramilitary unit, this kind of criminal report would not have been submitted to the district military prosecutor, would it?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't possibly know such a thing. They could have submitted their criminal report to whoever they liked. It was up to them to assess that sort of thing. It wasn't up to the prosecutor, and the prosecutor would not have been responsible for affecting this process in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the reasoning behind my question. We have someone who submits a report, in this case the Security Services Centre, civilian police. Now, it depended on them alone who they would be filing this report with, right, the senior prosecutor or the district military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and here it says clearly "The senior public prosecutor, Zenica."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Your Honours, can we please. I want to refer him briefly to Exhibit 882. I think the witness actually has a copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please go to page 16. I believe it's page 16. The larger one. This is page 1, and you need to go to page 16 in the B/C/S. Your Honours, it appears there is no translation. Fine. If we could please show this document in the Bosnian, right, okay, so that the witness can see the information there. Witness, this is your report dated the 22nd of August, 2007. I want you to look at this portion here with the blank or empty boxes, about midway down the page, "232/96, district military prosecutor, Travnik." And then we have four boxes in a row like that. You agree, right, all these four cases are in relation to the crime of murder, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is Article 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We have the names stated there, names of persons, but we don't know what particular event this is in relation to or who the victims are; we don't see that, do we?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this one thing, Witness. How could you then have written in your report, since obviously you had portions of the report that were incomplete, that there were no criminal reports that had to do with what had occurred in the village of Maline/Bikosi? You see that these are from Travnik, these cases, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These, I assume, came from the Travnik district military prosecutor. The date they were received, the next box, the 10th of November, 1996. That's right. There is the name of the suspect, but all the other information is missing. Therefore, it's possible that these cases were suspended or they may have been sent back to Travnik, according to this information. Date and place of crime, we don't have that. There's probably no information concerning that in the original record. Name of victim, we don't have that either. As long as it's not recorded, to me that suggests that the information was not contained in the original record. Why that is the case is not something that I can explain right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. Could we please put this document away for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Madam Vidovic, I just want to be reminded. There are two dates here, one on the third column and on the fifth column. The date on the third column, what does it signify?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this a question for me or for the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look? The columns are right there for you.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume -- well, I must say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go to the head of the table.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the head, it says "Date," and I think this is date of receipt, the date a certain case file was received. Senior public prosecutor, 1996, late 1995. Be that as it may, it's the date of receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The date on the fifth column with the name of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the date and place of crime, the date on which a crime occurred and the place where it occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. Could we please put this one away for the time being, and I want the witness to look at D709.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you see here is a report by the Military Police Battalion, dated the 20th of March, 1994, submitted to the Security Sector of the 3rd Corps. It was produced in Zenica, report on criminal reports filed. Could you please just have a look briefly under "C," the groups of persons that this comprises. You see that a total of 377 reports were filed, and under "B," 804 identified and 20 unidentified perpetrators. And now, under "D": "The structure of the crimes." You see that in relation to the crime of murder, there were 16 reports. And now please go to page 2 of the document. That is material for our purposes. In the English, it's page 2 as well. Could you please find where it says "War crimes." That's in the lower third of the page. You see it's the last thing we can see in the B/C/S page. If we could please lower the document so we can see the bottom of the page in the Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I repeat my question. Where is the war crimes in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking for it, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm trying to see if we're on the right page. My apologies, Your Honour. We are trying to track it down in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, take your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is page 3, three lines from the top, the third bullet point. You can see it, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you could read to yourself that this period pertains to the period of about one and a half year of activities of the Battalion of the Military Police. Have a look at this part concerning crimes against civilians, Article 142 of the SFRY Criminal Code. You can see that four criminal reports were submitted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The English says "3".

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I said "3", Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter said "4".

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say "3."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me -- well, we went through your document a few moments ago, and we found only two criminal reports submitted by the MP battalion in the whole of your report.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerns the following. I have to clarify something.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the break, I reviewed the tables, and I realised that in the table, when war crimes are concerned, there are separate case files of the former District Military Prosecutor's Office or the former Higher Military Prosecutor's Office. The tables that are part of the document dated the 24th of October, 2006, at page 2, the whole page contains the case files concerning war crimes. I also wanted to say that out of all of the suspects -- well, there were many more, in actual fact. For example, in table 3 -- sorry, in line 3, where the suspect is Opert, Azmahudin [phoen], well, there were more people involved and their names are not mentioned. All of the people in the table on this page are Bosniaks, Muslims, except for the last person mentioned in the last line. I wanted to offer that clarification concerning the questions so far. Then criminal reports, together with all of the evidence, if charges were pressed, all that should be contained in the court file. In that case, it could happen in the table that there are pieces of information missing, as was the case a minute ago, or, as in this specific case, if the criminal report submitted is specified as such in the register, the person submitting that request should be mentioned in the table. However, we can also see that in the tables we have, for example, "OBT Travnik" or "OVS Zenica," which means that that is the District Military Prosecutor's Office and the District Military Court, and in no case could they have submitted the criminal report. It is rather that the person who made the entry merely noted down who the case was received from or, rather, what institution it was transferred from. That would in turn mean that in the register, in the column the person or body who submitted the criminal report, we do not have that specific information. That is why there may be discrepancies or the issues such as the one you raise raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for your detailed explanation. Your Honour, I wish to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 888.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please have a look at D710. Witness, before you, you have a letter from the District Military Court in Travnik to the 3rd Corps Command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zenica. It has to do with the fact that the commander of the OG Bosanska Krajina believed that the cause for the increase of crime on the part of army members is the ineffectiveness of the Military Court, and the president of the Court is now explaining why. I would like you to have a look at the last page of the document, which has to do with your area. Could we please show the witness that part. It is page 4 in the English, page 4 in the English, the last paragraph. I wanted to ask you something about an important issue concerning the work of the judiciary at the time. It is stated here: "In closing down, we should like to mention in connection with the criminal reports, which as has been established, have not been received by this court, it may be asserted that the same are received by either the District Military Court in Zenica or by the District Military Court in Banja Luka." You can see here that Kemal Poricanin was the president of the Court. Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I have heard of that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You heard of him as being president of the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this entire line of questioning, and the relevance of this document -- because of the relevance of this document, Your Honour. This is not a document that this witness would have any knowledge about. It did not include a court that he was involved with. I believe any answers he might give in this regard are outside his purview and would be irrelevant. I just want to put an end to this at this point, Your Honour, especially considering I see that perhaps my learned colleague might wish to enter this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I got no interpretation, Judge. I didn't hear what Judge Lattanzi said. I didn't understand, at least. There was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just noting when I finished listening to the French translation. I think it was several minutes after Mr. Wood completed the presentation of his objection, and I needed to understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. I guess the moral or the lesson is that we should slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Understood, Your Honour. I would like to address the objection. The witness worked at the District Military Prosecutor's Office in Zenica, and mention is made of the criminal reports forwarded to Zenica. This is something that has to do with the operation of the Zenica Court and Prosecutor's Office, and the witness may certainly answer that. You will also remember that at the beginning of my cross-examination, I was asking questions about what he knows about the work of the war presidencies in exile. You will see that the court mentioned here is the District Court in Banja Luka. I just wanted to have all those facts straight to see how relevant it was for the whole matter, since I wanted to discuss with the witness whether criminal reports were sent not only to Zenica and Travnik, but also to such prosecutor's offices as shown here of the District Military Courts. That is the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before maybe Mr. Wood stands up, if he is going to, do I understand, Madam Vidovic, that Banja Luka is in exile?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not quite what I meant, Your Honour. I said that the War Presidency and the District Military Court of Banja Luka were in exile, and that is what I wanted to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I see the first page of the English, please. Okay. I must confess I just don't know how to rule on this objection, simply because I'm not following what is happening here. Do you follow, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also find it difficult to understand, so I think it is worthwhile spending a bit of time on all of these questions. So it might be better to carry on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My only problem is that there is an objection raised, and I've heard the objection, I've heard Madam Vidovic's explanation. I'm still in the dark. Maybe you will cast some light. Just say what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Your Honour, the second page of the document speaks of the writer of the document speculating that perhaps some files went to a place where they shouldn't have gone. Putting a question like that to this witness only invites him to speculate even further, first. And, secondly, this is 20 May 1993. It's the District Military Court in Travnik. This witness was not involved with that Court at any time, and 20 May 1993 is when he was in a different court. Additionally, Your Honour, this is -- as we know, the indictment period begins on 8 June 1993. For these reasons, this document can't conceivably be considered to be relevant, and any questions put to this witness will only lead to irrelevant answers. And that is the Prosecution's submission on this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, let me --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I may be of assistance. I don't need this document at all. We can put it away and I can put this question without it. I merely wanted Their Honours to have an example before them. First of all, I don't know how the Prosecutor can anticipate what my question would be. I only want the witness to clarify the issue of war presidencies and military prosecutors' offices in exile, and I can do that without the document. We can put it away now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we can do that, if we have the document, that would be very helpful, because I'm just a bit lost. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you worked in the so-called "War Presidency in exile." I would like to ask you this: It is true, is it not, that in Central Bosnia there were also military prosecutors' offices and war presidencies in exile active?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You never heard of a district military court in exile in Banja Luka; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, since this is the first time you've heard of it, you haven't gone through the archives of such prosecutors' offices and courts, in case there are such archives in existence and since you had no knowledge of such cases?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems I've been asked a question I cannot answer. I already answered in -- during the examination-in-chief, what was contained in the archives of the Cantonal Prosecutor's Office in Zenica that I headed. The organs you mentioned, the District Military Prosecutor's Office or Court of Banja Luka, well, we had no such documentation within the Cantonal Prosecutor's Office in Zenica, where I am the chief prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you something concerning criminal reports that were submitted by the Ministry of the Interior. Do you agree that before the war, during the war and after the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was common practice that the Minister of the Interior actually filed criminal reports in the first instance; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you about the period pertaining to the war and after that, since before the war, I was not at the same position. In essence, citizens submit reports in most of the cases, and they submit them to the Minister of the Interior. During the war, perhaps they were also submitting reports to the military police as well, and then they would initiate pre-trial proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we should clarify something. Did I understand you correctly that you said that the military police could also submit criminal reports to the Ministry -- sorry, to the Centre of Security Services? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I said that the citizens could inform or submit criminal reports to the Ministry of the Interior, that is, the civilian police, or to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the interpreters. If a perpetrator is unknown, in that situation wasn't there cooperation between the military and civilian police, if you know, or, rather, civilian and military bodies, to the extent that reports would be sent to the Minister of the Interior in order to try and establish who the perpetrator is?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I am not familiar with that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to show an official note of the District Military Court in Zenica. It's Exhibit number 252.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you can see the official note created in Zenica on the 12th of June, 1993. It concerns the bringing of corpses to the Prosecutor's Office from the lines held by the units of the 3rd Corps. It has to do with people from Ovnak and Susanj, as you can see. It seems that you were present during the on-site investigation. Is this your name, Muris Hadziselimovic?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is my name and I remember the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page in both versions so as to be able to see the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that it was signed by Investigating Judge of the District Military Court, Vlado Adamovic. You said you remember the event. Did the Investigating Judge Adamovic consult the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you. It's not an on-site investigation. Rather it is identification of the dead bodies that were brought to the Pathology Department of the Cantonal Hospital in Zenica. However, this judge headed the whole investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You obviously are familiar with this case. I would be correct, would I not, if I said that concerning these events in June 1993, in Susanj and Ovnak, there was an investigation by your Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure there was an investigation. This is one of the investigative measures that was conducted and that was headed by Judge Adamovic. Whether there was a full investigation on the events, I cannot tell you. I don't remember anyone being prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I put to you that even a sentence was handed down, would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if I was in charge of the case, not in any other case. It would be difficult for me to say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You're trying to tell me that you were not in charge of the case. However, in principle, would you agree with me that when the organs of the judiciary learn of such events, they are duty-bound to establish what had happened? They didn't merely attend the scene and made a list and leave?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was an investigative measure of identifying the persons brought in. We don't know where they were found, how they were killed, or anything else, for that matter. The only thing important at that point was to identify them, and an external examination of the corpses was made. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I don't think I can press this any further. I would like to ask you something about your witness statement. In paragraph 15 of your statement to the investigators of the OTP, you described the discovery of 22 unlogged cases. These were not registered in the registers. You subsequently found that at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are on the same page, it is about the cases found in the archives. As far as I recall, it was an archives of the one of the former Municipal Prosecutors' Offices where -- I can't recall the exact figure, but between 10 and 20 cases which had not been entered into any of the registers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 17 of your statement, you say that a damaged party gave you a call recently, inquiring about their case, and you also stated that that case was something you did not find at all in your registers; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say I don't remember specifically, but if that's what I said, then it must be that way. It's possible that I made a suggestion to that party to file a criminal report with us so that we may have reason to investigate the case. If that's what this is about, then it must be that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. How can you say, then -- you have all those boxes of cases that when filed, people were calling you on the phone, "What's going on with my file," and then you simply say, "Well, it's not there. Can you resubmit that, please." And then how can you be telling us that you have accurate registers containing all the criminal reports that were filed?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The registers are accurate, and these two facts confirm that. When the archives were tidied up, and this is something that I had requested -- this was just before the request was made by the OTP to me -- this particular box was found along with all the other items lying about. Everything save for that one box was fully recorded. So this box is an exception confirming the rule. Everything that ever reached the Prosecutor's Office was recorded. Of course, I can't be expected to answer for something that someone, whoever was responsible in that particular Prosecutor's Office, failed to do, something they didn't record in the register. Everything that was taken over, all the documents from all the Prosecutors' Offices that I mentioned, was recorded in these registers, with the exception of this one box. And as for the criminal report that you asked me about, I have to say that that occurrence was never recorded by any of the prosecutors. I checked the books, first of all, and then we had not a single fact to go on in relation to that case. I made a suggestion to the party in question to file a criminal report -- to submit a criminal report so that we might finally find ourselves in possession of some facts, and then for the prosecutor to launch an investigation. I requested that so that we might be able to record that and then press on with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It looks like this is not my day today. There's a concept of boxes that's being introduced in the discussion. I'm not quite sure -- and both of you seem to be understanding each other. How do these boxes come in? The first answer had been: "I have to say I don't remember specifically, but if that's what I said, then it must be that way. It's possible that I made a suggestion to the party to file a criminal report with us so that we may have reason to investigate the case. If that's what this is about, then it must be that way." Then the next question says: "That's right. How can you say, then, have all those boxes of cases that, when filed, people were calling on the phone, 'What's going on with my file' ..." That's the first time I hear of a box.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may clarify, the witness made a statement to the OTP, to the investigators of the OTP in March -- or, rather, in May 2007. In that statement, he describes, and I can quote if you like me to, the discovery of these 22 unlogged cases in a box somewhere in the archives of the Prosecutor's Office. That's paragraph 15 of the statement. You can check if you have a copy. And then next, paragraph 17, the witness says: "Three days ago, we received a criminal report for a crime committed against a civilian in Zavidovici in 1992." And then the witness goes on to say: "The brother of the victim contacted us." So it's in that portion of the statement that the witness talks about that. This is an event that was never recorded in any of the registers, and that's why I'm asking the witness these questions, my objective being to ascertain this: There were obviously certain cases that were not recorded, not registered by the Prosecutor's Office. They had them right there, the case files, but the case files were never registered. So that is the purpose behind my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm with you, it's just that paragraph 15 and 17 do not talk about boxes. They talk of unlogged cases, but I -- and the logging there is not even -- but that's fine. Now I'm with you, at least, whether there is a box or not, no boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see the word "box" in paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to point that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Box, box, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how it was interpreted. I said "a box containing 22 case files."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the reference here is probably to boxes in which these case files were physically kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Just before you re-examine, Mr. Wood, I know that you answered to this question, but I just want to ask you the question I'm going to ask you because of the answer you gave at the beginning of your cross-examination. What are war presidencies in exile, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were civilian authorities for those municipalities from which they were expelled. For example, the Kotor Varos Municipality, which is my municipality, I hail from that municipality, I was elected to the War Presidency by the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on roughly the same date I was appointed deputy military prosecutor. These war presidencies, in theory, at least, had certain powers, but in practice they had no particular role, other than to organise people who were expelled from a certain area, to list those people, the citizens, and, in any way they could, to help these people survive in their new areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, okay, I hear you now and I understand better now. Now, when you said, in answer to a question by Madam Vidovic, that it is the first time you hear about this War Presidency, were you talking specifically about the Banja Luka War Presidency? Is that the one that you were hearing about for the first time, or what were you saying when you said: "This is the first time I hear about that," and Madam Vidovic didn't pursue that point, she just left it there? Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, the question was about the District Military Court of Banja Luka, and that was the first time I'd heard of it. It wasn't about the War Presidency. I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If Exhibit 881 could be shown, please. And this is in regard to the table. So if we go to page 6 in the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziselimovic, the Defence attorney asked you about 236/95, which is almost exactly in the middle of that page. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber, what is the referring agency for 236/95? I see that it's being highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that it was Security Services Centre, Zenica, which means civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could go to page 9 in the Bosnian, and I want to ask you about entries alluded to by the Defence attorney regarding Enver Hadzihasanovic and Besim Spahic. That's 014/2001. If you could scroll down to where those names are listed. I don't see them on this page, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance, it's actually page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hadziselimovic, do you see the file 014/2001?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And 015/2001? I'm sorry, I misspoke. 015/01. Mr. Hadziselimovic, what does "2001" indicate at the end of "014"?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that this was recorded in the register in the year 2001, number 14 and number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if you could look to the second cell in the row, where it says "Ki 33/01", what does that indicate, Mr. Hadziselimovic?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the way the Court categorises this file, and the numbers are 33/01 and 37/01. This is a court reference number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what, specifically, does "Ki" indicate?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Criminal investigation," which is as good as a case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If we could go back to page 1 in the English and the Bosnian of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I want to draw your attention in particular to Roman numeral I. Now, that reads: "That data that we have submitted in attachment, relating to files found in the Archives of the Zenica District Military Prosecution ..." And it continues, as you can see there. Does this indicate, Mr. Hadziselimovic, that the documents listed in the table attached here or the files are only files that are found in the Zenica Military District Prosecution register?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that were shown, the two case files, should be cases for the senior public prosecutor in Zenica, because this comprises the entire archives, the district military prosecutor in Zenica and the senior public prosecutor in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: My question is more specific, though, Mr. Hadziselimovic. As to the table attached to this document, are these excerpts taken from, as is written here, the Zenica District Military Prosecution archive -- or logbook?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, but I am not certain that this is 100 per cent accurate. It may as well be that this comprises the archives of the senior public prosecutor as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention to page 2 in the Bosnian, page 2 in the English. If you could scroll to the top. Could you read that sentence out, sir, the very top sentence, the only sentence on the page above the table?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which sentence in the English, Mr. Wood?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I believe we'll have to go to the next page in the English to see that sentence, Mr. President. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reads: "List of selected files from the Archives of the Zenica District Military Prosecutor," illegible, "21 to 24 August 2006. Mission. Mission from the 21st to 24th of August."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: We saw a document earlier introduced by the Defence that indicated -- that referred to the murder of Paul Godal and some others. Perhaps we could just bring that up. That's Exhibit 887. Now, we see at the top of that page, it says "Senior Public Prosecutor's Office." Does that indicate where this was sent, Mr. Hadziselimovic?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the address to which it was supposed to be sent. I have nothing indicating that it ever got there, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So if we put these two documents together, if, as is written, the table at the end of 881 is only excerpts of a list of selected files from the archives of the Zenica District Military Prosecution, would there be any reason that a criminal report sent to the Senior Public Prosecutor's Office in Zenica would appear in the table at the end of 881?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, we saw, Mr. Hadziselimovic, that a certain sentence was written at the end of Exhibit 881, right before the table, and that sentence indicated that the criminal reports listed in the table were taken from the archives of the Zenica District Military Prosecution registers. We see, on this document, that a criminal report was sent to the Senior Public Prosecutor's Office in Zenica. So if the table at the end of 881 only lists documents or criminal reports from the Zenica District Military Prosecutor's Office, would there be any reason that these criminal reports would appear in the table at the end of 881 if what is written is true and they were sent to the Public Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is stated that the list of files is from the Zenica prosecutor, district military prosecutor, then it should be right, but there could have been a change in the jurisdiction, so I have to assume that the senior public prosecutor, for example, said, "This is not within our jurisdiction. We are forwarding the case to the district military prosecutor." And then this file would be transferred to the district military prosecutor and it could turn up in this table. That is the only explanation that I think is possible in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And generally speaking, sir, on Roman II of 881 and 882, and we could bring those up, but we need not, Your Honour, you assert that you did a search of the archives and the registers and found that there were no criminal reports filed for the events that were specified by the OTP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In carrying out that search, sir, did you and your staff rely only on the registers or did you also check the individual files for these individual cases?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We relied primarily on our records, because if a case was tried, then all the documents should be in the Court for us to be able to inspect a certain case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So, for example, if there are -- if there was a case of Article 36 murder that was found in the register, what did your staff do to make sure that that Article 36 case for murder did not include, as in 2(1), the murder of 25 civilians or the murder of the VRS prisoners at -- in Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one runs a check by using the names of those killed, the injured parties, and then we're 100 per cent certain about our records. But it's not just the names of suspects that are looked at here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What else is looked at?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One looks at the names of the suspects involved, the names of the injured parties, the time of submission, the relevant prosecutor's office that was in charge of a certain case. It was mostly cases from that other kind of register, unidentified perpetrator, or the juvenile perpetrator, under-age perpetrator. For example, when you have a KT record and you don't have a perpetrator, and in that case what you use to run this search is the names of the persons who are the actual victims. There is no other way to conduct a search than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And are those the criteria that were used in asserting, as you did, in Roman II of both letters that there were no criminal reports filed for these particular events?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, finally, I want to ask you some questions about the box of 22 files that was referenced in your witness statement. Was this the only set of files you found that had not actually been logged in any logbook?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And in the process of going through these files, how many files did you find that were actually logged in the various logbooks?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a little difficult to say off-the-cuff like that. If you look at "unidentified perpetrator," there may be about 40.000 files, all the rest, between 30.000 and 40.000 [Realtime transcript read in error "13.000 and 14.000"] case files.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So we're talking about, then -- I'm sorry, I want to clarify here. Did you say 13.000 and 14.000?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So we're talking about 22 case files out of 30 to 40.000, then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Hadziselimovic, if you recall, what did these particular cases, these 22, deal with?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were criminal reports concerning unidentified perpetrators, about the shelling of Tesanj Municipality and parts of Doboj Municipality by the Serb aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And one final question. You referred, in page 46, line 1, when we were speaking of the case file involving Enver Hadzihasanovic, you said the BH organs forwarded it to The Hague Tribunal. Do you know, Mr. Hadziselimovic, from where the "rules of the road" case file against Enver Hadzihasanovic originated?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sent by the senior public prosecutor in Zenica, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wood. Judge. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to put to you. This relates to those 22 cases which had not been recorded. Have I understood you correctly that this pertained to the period running from 1992, when you were not yet working for the military tribunal of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This pertained to the period between 1992 and 1995, and I don't know the exact date when those events occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about the cases, those cases that were not recorded, pertain to that period running from 1992 and 1995. Is that what you're saying? In other words, during this period you cannot confirm either that your office was running efficiently and, therefore, that all cases were registered, all criminal reports were being recorded; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe the explanation was not sufficiently clear. That particular box was found in the same place where other documents were being kept, too, and this is something that the prosecutor in Zenica had taken over from the former municipal prosecutor in Tesanj. When the Cantonal Prosecutor's Office in Zenica was set up, all the Municipal Public Prosecutors' Offices were abolished. That was when we took over all the documentation from all the municipal prosecutors. All the cases were recorded in the register, where receipt was recorded. And when the archives were searched, when we wanted to tidy up the archives so we might know what exactly we had there, it was then that the box was found containing these 22 case files. These case files were not recorded in the register of the Tesanj municipal prosecutor. When we ascertained that, we duly recorded them and pursued those case files. When I say "we," I mean the cantonal prosecutor of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what we are interested in is as follows: If this period running from 1993 to 1995, you are able to confirm to us that your office was being run efficiently and that you were able to record anything coming in, whenever there were any criminal reports, that you were actually able to record all of this?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One other point. During her cross-examination, Mrs. Vidovic put a question to you that concerned reports. She was making an assumption, if I remember correctly, and she mentioned reports that might have reached you which would have involved paramilitaries. And if I remember correctly, you said, "I cannot answer that question because I don't know anything about these reports, and I don't know whom these reports were sent to." Have I remembered all of this correctly?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like to know something else. As far as you're concerned, if you yourself, working for the military tribunal, if you had received reports which had to do with the involvement of paramilitary forces, would you have felt that these reports fell within your jurisdiction or not, or came under your jurisdiction or not?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the law, the jurisdiction was determined in such a way that the military prosecutors, military courts, had jurisdiction over anyone who was a member of the armed forces. There was no mention there of any paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to have any other questions, Mr. Wood, arising from those questions by the Judge?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a brief question. Further cross-examination by Ms. Vidovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm sure you'll agree, the 22 case files that remained in that box, under the law they had to be recorded in the registers; right?

utterances.speaker: MURIS HADZISELIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, and that follows from my answer. These had to be recorded or registered, but they were not. It wasn't until 12 years later that we recorded them and entered them into all the logs. Since these are apparently cases involving war crimes, we shall do our best to investigate these cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Sir, this brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to testify. You are now excused and you may stand down. And travel back home safely. Thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank you, the Prosecutor and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have to keep you waiting, but -- thank you, thank you so much. The Trial Chamber hereby now renders its decision on the Prosecution's fifth motion for leave to amend its exhibit list which was filed on the 7th of November, 2007. In its motion, the Prosecution requests leave to amend its Rule 65 ter exhibit list by the addition of 13 documents which are attached as Annex B to the motion. The Prosecution argues that it is in the interests of justice to allow the addition of these 13 proposed exhibits, as they "negate the validity of document MFI 651 that was used by the defence during the cross-examination of a key witness," namely, the witness Goran Krcmar. The Prosecution argues that it should be permitted to add the proposed exhibits to its list, as MFI 651 is directly contradictory to a fact which the Prosecution seeks to prove, and that it will be unable to add these proposed exhibits to its 65 ter exhibit list at a later stage should the Defence tender this document for admission into evidence during the Defence case. The Defence, in its response of the 21st of November, 2007, argues that it is not in the interests of justice to allow the addition of the proposed exhibits, as the correct stage at which to deal with this matter is if the Defence bring a witness to deal with this document during the Defence case, and that the key document among the proposed exhibits carries little or no probative value in the absence of a witness called by the Prosecution to testify as to the error which may have been made in MFI 651. The Trial Chamber recalls that it may grant a motion requesting amendment of a 65 ter exhibit list where it is in the interests of justice and in balancing the Prosecution's duty to present the available evidence to prove its case with the right of the accused to have adequate time and facilities to prepare a defence. The Trial Chamber may also take into account additional criteria, including whether the proposed evidence is prima facie relevant and of probative to the issues in the indictment and where a good cause for amending the 65 ter exhibit list has been shown. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber recalls that there is a difference between the admission of a document into evidence as an exhibit and the inclusion of the document on the 65 ter exhibit list, as in the latter case the Trial Chamber does not need to assess the relevance and probative value of such documents, provided it is satisfied that the party does not submit documents that are obviously irrelevant. Having considered the arguments advanced by the Prosecution in its motion and by the Defence in its response, the Trial Chamber finds that the proposed exhibits are prima facie relevant to the Prosecution case and that the Prosecution has shown good cause for the amendment of its 65 ter exhibit list. Therefore, the Trial Chamber finds that it is in the interests of justice to allow the addition of the 13 proposed exhibits to the Prosecution's 65 ter exhibit list and pursuant to Rule 54 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, hereby grants the evidence. I'm sorry to have kept the parties for too long. Court adjourned. We have a problem. We don't know whether we're sitting in the morning tomorrow or in the afternoon. We are told that we will be notified sometime perhaps later in the day. I want to suspect that we will sit in the morning. Court adjourned on that uncertain note.
